[b0] (explanation)
Two lines are parallel when they run side by side and never meet, no matter how far they are extended. You can tell they are parallel because they keep the same distance apart all along their length. In a diagram, parallel lines are often marked with matching little arrows.

In this section you will learn how to draw a line through a given point that is parallel to a given line, using only a ruler, a set square, and a pencil. The set square is the triangle-shaped tool with a right angle (a 90° corner) at one end. It does the important job for us: because its straight edge stays fixed against the ruler, we can slide it along without turning it, and the lines it draws stay parallel.

Here is the idea behind the method. When you draw any straight line and then draw another line that cuts across it (called a transversal), the two lines are parallel exactly when the angles they make with that crossing line are equal. In the construction below we use this fact in a simple mechanical way: sliding a set square along a ruler keeps its edge at the same angle the whole time, so the line you draw is always at the same angle to the ruler — and that guarantees the new line is parallel to the first.

[b1] (worked_example)
Worked example: Construct a line through the point P that is parallel to the line AB.

Step 1 — Draw the given line AB and mark the point P anywhere off it. Keep P a sensible distance away, not too close and not too far.

Step 2 — Place your set square so that one of its straight edges lies exactly on top of the line AB.

Step 3 — Keeping the set square pressed down firmly, place your ruler against the other straight edge of the set square so the ruler touches it along its whole length. Hold the ruler very still.

Step 4 — While holding the ruler in place, slide the set square along the ruler towards P. Do not let it twist or lift: it must stay pressed against the ruler the whole time.

Step 5 — When the top edge of the set square reaches P, keep it there and draw a straight line through P along that edge. This new line is parallel to AB.

Step 6 — Mark the new line with a little arrow (the same style of arrow as on AB) to show the two lines are parallel.

Because you slid the set square without turning it, the edge you drew along stayed at exactly the same angle to the ruler as the line AB was. That equal angle is what guarantees the two lines are parallel.

[b2] (explanation)
Let us look at the reasoning once more, because it is the whole secret of the construction.

Imagine a line CD drawn across the line AB (so CD cuts AB at some point). Now imagine the same line CD drawn across your new line. If the angle that CD makes with AB is exactly the same as the angle that CD makes with the new line, then the two lines are parallel. This is what we depend on.

In the set-square method, the ruler plays the part of CD: it is the fixed reference line that both AB and your new line cross. When you slide the set square along the ruler without turning it, you are drawing a line that meets the ruler at exactly the same angle that AB meets the ruler. Same crossing line, same angle — so the two lines must be parallel.

A useful check when you finish: parallel lines are the same distance apart everywhere. Use your ruler to measure the gap between AB and the new line at two different places. If both measurements are equal, your construction has worked.

[p0] (practice)
Draw a straight horizontal line and label it AB. Choose a point P above the line, about halfway along it. Using only a ruler and a set square, construct a line through P that is parallel to AB. Explain in one sentence why the method works.
answer: You slide the set square along the ruler without turning it, so the new line meets the ruler at the same angle as AB. Because the new line and AB make equal angles with the same crossing line (the ruler), the two lines are parallel. Check by measuring the gap in two places — the distances should be equal.

[p1] (practice)
Line XY is drawn slanting downwards. Construct a line through a point Q, placed below and to the right of the line, that is parallel to XY. What single thing must you avoid doing while sliding the set square, and why does that matter?
answer: You must avoid letting the set square twist or lift away from the ruler while you slide it. If it twists, its edge no longer keeps the same angle to the ruler, so the line you draw would meet the ruler at a different angle and would not be parallel to XY.

[p2] (practice)
Two students each draw a line through point P. Student A slides the set square along the ruler without turning it. Student B turns the set square a little as it slides. Only one of the two lines is guaranteed parallel to the original line. Which student, and why?
answer: Student A's line is guaranteed parallel, because keeping the set square at the same angle to the ruler makes the new line meet the ruler at the same angle as the original line. Student B turned the set square, which changes that angle, so the line is not guaranteed to be parallel.

[b0] (explanation)
An angle of 60° is one you can build with just a ruler and a pair of compasses, using two arcs of the same radius. The key idea: when you swing an arc of a fixed radius from a point, every point on that arc is the same distance from the centre. Two arcs of the *same* radius from two different centres will meet at a point that is that same distance from both — and that equal spacing is what makes the angle 60°.

The construction needs just three moves. You can follow them on fig-14.

[b1] (worked_example)
**Constructing a 60° angle at B, along the line BC**

1. **Draw the line.** Draw a line segment and mark a point B on it where the angle will sit. Mark the far end of the line C. Set your compasses to any convenient radius — it can be any size that fits comfortably on your page.

2. **First arc from B.** With the compass point on B, draw an arc that cuts the line BC at a point. Call that point X. (On fig-14 this is the long arc swung from B through X.)

3. **Second arc from X.** Keep the compasses at exactly the *same* radius — do not change the setting. Now put the compass point on X and draw another arc that cuts the first arc. Call the point where the two arcs cross A. (On fig-14 this is the shorter arc swung from X cutting the first.)

4. **Join A to B.** Draw a straight line from B to A.

The angle between line BC and line BA is exactly 60°. Because both arcs were drawn with the same radius, the distance from B to A equals the distance from B to X, which equals the distance from X to A — so the triangle BAX has all three sides equal, and a triangle with three equal sides has all three angles 60°.

[b0] (explanation)
When we collect a lot of numbers, they can be hard to read. Statistics is the way we organise those numbers so they start to tell us something useful. One of the most helpful tools for doing this is a table.

A table takes rows of information and lines them up in columns, so you can see at a glance what is there. For example, suppose a class counted how many books each student read in a month. Instead of listing twenty separate numbers, we can put them in a table like this:

| Number of books read | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|----------------------|---|---|---|---|
| Number of students   | 4 | 7 | 6 | 3 |

To read a table, you ask yourself simple questions and let the numbers answer them.

Question: How many students read exactly 3 books? Look down the "Number of books read" row until you find 3. The number underneath it, 7, tells you that 7 students read 3 books.

Question: How many students were counted altogether? Add every number in the bottom row: 4 + 7 + 6 + 3 = 20 students.

Question: How many students read 4 or 5 books? Add the students in those two columns: 6 + 3 = 9 students.

So a table lets you compare groups, find totals, and answer questions quickly. The columns and rows are your signposts — always read the headings first so you know what each number is counting.

[b1] (worked_example)
Example — Favourite fruits

A shop asked its customers which fruit they liked most and recorded the answers in this table:

| Fruit      | Apple | Banana | Mango | Orange |
|------------|-------|--------|-------|--------|
| Customers  | 12    | 8      | 15    | 5      |

Let's read a few facts from it.

Step 1: Which fruit was liked most?
Look for the biggest number in the "Customers" row. The biggest is 15, which sits under Mango. So mango was the favourite fruit.

Step 2: How many customers chose banana or orange?
Add the customers for those two fruits: 8 + 5 = 13 customers.

Step 3: How many customers answered altogether?
Add the whole "Customers" row: 12 + 8 + 15 + 5 = 40 customers.

Step 4: How many more customers chose apple than orange?
The apple column has 12 and the orange column has 5. The difference is 12 − 5 = 7 more customers chose apple.

Notice how each answer came straight from reading the numbers in the table. The headings told us what the numbers meant, and the numbers answered our questions.

[b2] (explanation)
To interpret a table confidently, use these three steps every time:

1. Read the headings. The row and column headings tell you what the numbers are counting. Without them, numbers have no meaning.

2. Find the right column or row. Put your finger on the heading you are interested in and follow it to the number you need.

3. Do the arithmetic the question asks for. Sometimes you just read one number. Sometimes you add columns together, or subtract one from another to find a difference.

A table is a summary: it takes a messy list of data and turns it into answers you can find. Once you can read a table, you can interpret statistical data — which simply means turning the numbers back into a clear description of what they show.

| Sport    | Football | Basketball | Tennis | Swimming |
|----------|----------|------------|--------|----------|
| Members  | 18       | 10         | 6      | 14       |

(a) How many members play tennis?
(b) How many members were asked altogether?
(c) Which sport is played by the most members?
(d) How many more members play football than basketball?
answer: (a) 6 members play tennis. (b) 18 + 10 + 6 + 14 = 48 members. (c) Football, with 18 members. (d) 18 − 10 = 8 more members play football than basketball.

(c) How many more baskets did Tree D give than Tree A?
answer: (a) Tree C, with 7 baskets. (b) 12 + 7 = 19 baskets. (c) 15 − 9 = 6 more baskets.

Explanation:
"Every day you meet information — numbers, names, scores. When you count the boys and girls in your class, you are gathering information. When you write those counts down so you can see them clearly, you are organising it. The method of collecting and organising information so that it can be understood and used is called statistics.

Statistics exists for a purpose. We do not collect and organise information just to fill pages. We do it so that the information can tell us something — how many, which is more, which is less, and what to do next. For example, the class register is a record of who is present and absent each day. Counting and recording that information lets you know how many learners came to school and helps the school plan for the day. That is the purpose of statistics: to gather and arrange information so we can answer questions and make decisions from it."

Worked example:
"Suppose your teacher wants to know how many boys and how many girls are in your class of 40 learners. 
Step 1 — Collect the information: You count the boys. There are 22. You count the girls. There are 18. Counting is collecting.
Step 2 — Organise the information: You write the counts in a small table.

Boys | 22
Girls | 18

Now the information is arranged, and at a glance you can see there are more boys than girls, and that together they make 40 (22 + 18 = 40). This whole process — counting and writing the results in order — is an example of statistics, and its purpose is to turn a jumble of counting into information you can read and use."

A pyramid is named by the shape of its base. The base is the flat face the pyramid stands on, and the top point where all the sloping faces meet is called the apex. Because the base can be different shapes, there are several pyramids, each one named after its base.

A triangular based pyramid (also called a tetrahedron) has a triangle as its base. It has 4 faces, 6 edges and 4 vertices. A square based pyramid has a square base, and has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices. A pentagonal based pyramid has a pentagon as its base, and has 6 faces, 10 edges and 6 vertices. A rectangular based pyramid has a rectangle as its base, and has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.

Can you see the pattern? A pyramid with a base that has n sides always has n + 1 faces, 2n edges and n + 1 vertices. For example, a square base has 4 sides, so the pyramid has 4 + 1 = 5 faces, 2 × 4 = 8 edges and 4 + 1 = 5 vertices — which is exactly what the table above shows.

[b1] (explanation)
A cone is different from a pyramid. Instead of a polygon base with several straight sloping faces, a cone has just one curved face that narrows smoothly to the top point, called the apex, and one flat circular face at the base.

So a cone has:
- two faces — one curved face and one flat face,
- one edge (the circular rim where the curved face meets the flat base),
- one vertex (the apex, the point at the top).

Remember to keep a cone separate from a pyramid in your mind: a pyramid's faces are all flat triangles meeting at the apex, while a cone's side is a single curved surface.

When we want to answer a question like "Which colour do most students in my class like best?" or "How many children are in each family?", we first have to collect the data — that is, gather the facts or numbers. We can collect data by counting, by asking people (a questionnaire), by watching, or by recording what we observe. Once the data is collected, it usually looks like a long, messy list. To understand it, we need to organise it. One of the best ways is to build a frequency table. A frequency table shows us each different value and how many times it appears. That "how many times" is called the frequency.

Here is the simple idea behind a frequency table: we take every piece of data, and for each value we make a mark. We often use tally marks — four vertical strokes, with the fifth drawn across them as a diagonal line, so we can count quickly in groups of five. After we have marked every piece of data, we count the marks for each value and write the total. That total is the frequency.

When the table is finished, we can interpret it — we can read the table to answer questions about the data, such as which value is the most common, which is the least common, or how many pieces of data there are altogether (the total of all the frequencies).

When we want to answer a question like "Which colour do most students in my class like best?" or "How many children are in each family?", we first have to collect the data — that is, gather the facts or numbers. We can collect data by counting, by asking people (a questionnaire), by watching, or by recording what we observe. Once the data is collected, it usually looks like a long, messy list. To understand it, we need to organise it. One of the best ways is to build a frequency table. A frequency table shows us each different value and how many times it appears. That "how many times" is called the frequency.

Here is the simple idea behind a frequency table: we take every piece of data, and for each value we make a mark. We often use tally marks — four vertical strokes, with the fifth drawn across them as a diagonal line, so we can count quickly in groups of five. After we have marked every piece of data, we count the marks for each value and write the total. That total is the frequency.

[b0] (explanation) Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, presenting, analyzing and interpreting data. The word data sits at the heart of it all, so let's be clear about what data means. Data are facts or information collected for a particular purpose. The number of pupils in your class, the scores you got in your last test, or the amount of rain that fell each day last week are all examples of data. Each is a set of facts gathered for a reason — to answer a question or find something out. Wherever facts are gathered for a purpose, statistics is at work. [b1] (explanation) Why do we need statistics? Because it helps us to do five important things: (a) Collect information — bring facts together in one place. (b) Organize information — put the facts in order so they are easy to read and handle. (c) Compare information — look at two or more sets of facts side by side. (d) Make decisions — use the facts to choose what to do. (e) Present information clearly — show the facts in a way that others can understand. These five are the purpose of statistics: it turns scattered facts into useful, clear information that helps us decide and act. [b2] (worked_example) Example. Your class wants to know how many pupils walk to school. First you collect information by asking every pupil how they travel. Then you organize information by counting how many walk, how many ride a bicycle, and how many are dropped off by car. Now you can compare information to see which way most pupils travel, and present it clearly in a small table. Finally, you can make a decision — for instance, whether the school should ask for more bicycle racks. Title: "Bisecting a Line Segment" Explanation block text: "To **bisect** a line segment means to cut it into two equal halves. When you bisect the segment $AB$, you are finding the point $M$ exactly in the middle of it, so that the two halves $AM$ and $MB$ are equal: $AM = MB$. You do this with a pair of compasses and a ruler — the same equipment you used to draw lines. The line that splits $AB$ in half also meets it at a right angle, so this construction gives you both a midpoint and a perpendicular." Worked example text: "**Construct the bisector of the line segment $AB$.** 1. Open your pair of compasses so that the radius is about three quarters of the length of $AB$ (see fig-10). 2. Place the sharp point of the compasses on $A$ and draw two arcs — one above and one below the middle of $AB$. 3. **Without changing the radius**, place the sharp point on $B$ and draw two more arcs so that they cut the first arcs at $P$ (above) and $Q$ (below), as in fig-11. 4. Join $P$ to $Q$ with a ruler (fig-12). 5. The line $PQ$ crosses $AB$ at $M$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $AM = MB$, and $PQ$ meets $AB$ at a right angle, $90^\\circ$." That's the worked example. Answer: "Keeping the same radius makes the two pairs of arcs cross at points $P$ and $Q$ such that the line through them passes through the midpoint of $AB$. Because of this, a circle has its own set of named parts. Learning these names lets you describe circles precisely and get ready to measure them. Here are the main parts of a circle and what each one means. The centre is the fixed point exactly in the middle of the circle. Every other part of the circle is named in relation to it. We often label it with a letter, such as O. The circumference is the distance all the way around the circle — it is the circle's outer boundary, the curved rim itself. The radius (plural: radii) is any straight line that joins the centre to a point on the circumference. Every radius of a circle has the same length. If you double the radius, you get the diameter. The diameter is a straight line that passes through the centre and touches the circumference at both ends. The diameter is twice the length of the radius, and every diameter divides the circle into two equal halves. A chord is a straight line that joins two points on the circumference. The diameter is the longest possible chord, because it is the only chord that passes through the centre. An arc is part of the circumference. A small part is called a minor arc, and the larger remaining part is called a major arc. [b0] (explanation)
When an algebraic expression contains several operations, you work through them in a fixed order. This order is the same one you use with numbers:

1. Do whatever is inside **brackets** first.
2. Then do **multiplication** and **division** from left to right.
3. Finally do **addition** and **subtraction** from left to right.

For example, in the expression \(5 + 3 \times 2x\), there are no brackets, so you multiply before you add:
\(5 + 3 \times 2x = 5 + 6x\).
The answer is \(5 + 6x\) — you cannot add 5 and 6x because they are not like terms.

If we put brackets in, the order changes. In \((5 + 3) \times 2x\), you work out the bracket first:
\((5 + 3) \times 2x = 8 \times 2x = 16x\).

So brackets can change the meaning of an expression completely. Always clear them out first.

[b1] (explanation)
To **remove a bracket**, multiply each term inside the bracket by what sits in front of it. This is called expanding the bracket.

\(3(2x + 4) = 3 \times 2x + 3 \times 4 = 6x + 12\)

When there is a minus sign in front of the bracket, it multiplies every term inside, so every sign flips:
\(- (3x - 5) = -3x + 5\)

Here is a longer simplification that puts everything together:
\[
2(3x + 1) - (x - 4)
\]
Remove both brackets:
\[
= 6x + 2 - x + 4
\]
Collect the like terms (the \(x\) terms, then the numbers):
\[
= (6x - x) + (2 + 4) = 5x + 6
\]

Always simplify fully so no like terms are left over.

[b2] (explanation)
Algebra is useful for solving **word problems**. To turn words into an algebraic expression, follow these steps:

1. Choose a letter to stand for the unknown amount.
2. Translate each phrase into a piece of algebra:

   - "five more than a number" means \(x + 5\)

   - "the sum of a number and four" means \(x + 4\)
3. Combine the pieces using the order of operations and brackets.

Here is an example. "A number is multiplied by 3, then 7 is added to the result." The number is \(x\), so:
\[
\text{result} = 3x + 7
\]

Brackets matter in word problems too. "The sum of a number and 4, all multiplied by 2" is written as \(2(x + 4)\), not \(2x + 4\). The words "the sum of ... all multiplied by" tell you to add first, so the addition goes inside the bracket.

- **Diameter**: a straight line that passes through the centre and touches the circumference at both ends. It is twice as long as the radius.
- **Chord**: a straight line joining any two points on the circumference. A chord does not have to pass through the centre.
- **Arc**: part of the circumference — a curved piece of the circle's boundary.
- **Segment**: the region inside the circle bounded by a chord and the arc it cuts off. (Picture the piece "cut off" from the rest of the circle.)
- **Sector**: the region inside the circle bounded by two radii and the arc between their ends. It looks like a slice or a wedge of the circle.
- **Tangent**: a straight line that touches the circumference at exactly one point and does not cross into the circle.

[b1] (worked_example)
Let us name the parts on a circle you can picture clearly.

Think of a circle with a point C in its very middle. From C, draw a straight line out to a point A on the circle's edge. This line CA is a **radius**, because it runs from the centre to the circumference.

Now draw another straight line from a point B on the circle, straight through the centre C, to a point D on the other side. The whole line BD passes through the centre and meets the circle at both ends, so BD is a **diameter**. Notice BD is made of two radii placed end to end, which is why a diameter is twice a radius.

The distance all the way around the circle from A, round and back to A, is the **circumference**. Take just the curved piece of the edge from A to B — that curved piece is an **arc**.

Join A and B with a straight line inside the circle. That line is a **chord** (here it does not pass through the centre, so it is not a diameter). The chord AB together with the arc AB closes off a region inside the circle — that region is a **segment**.

Now draw a straight line from the centre C to A, and another from C to B. These two radii, CA and CB, together with the arc AB between their ends, enclose a wedge-shaped region — that region is a **sector**.

Finally, imagine a straight line that just touches the circle at point A, resting against the edge without entering it. That line is a **tangent** to the circle at A.

So in one circle you have: the centre C, a radius CA, a diameter BD, the circumference around the edge, an arc AB, a chord AB, a segment between chord AB and arc AB, a sector between radii CA and CB and arc AB, and a tangent touching at A.

[p1] (practice)

answer: Radius.

[p2] (practice)
3. How does a diameter compare in length with a radius of the same circle?
answer: The diameter is twice as long as the radius.

[p3] (practice)
4. A straight line joining any two points on the circumference of a circle is called a __________. When must this line also be a diameter?
answer: A chord; it is also a diameter when it passes through the centre.

[p4] (practice)

(a) A straight line that touches the circumference at exactly one point.
(b) A curved piece of the circumference.
(c) A region bounded by two radii and the arc between them.
(d) A region bounded by a chord and the arc it cuts off.
answer: (a) tangent, (b) arc, (c) sector, (d) segment.

[p5] (practice)
6. In one circle, the radius is 5 cm. What is the length of the diameter? Explain your answer.
answer: 10 cm, because the diameter is twice the radius (2 × 5 cm = 10 cm).

Some shapes are solid: they have length, breadth and height, so they take up space. These are called **three-dimensional** shapes or **solid shapes**. A cube of sugar, a drink can and a match box are all solid shapes.

To describe a solid shape we talk about its **faces**, its **edges** and its **vertices** (one is a *vertex*).

- A **face** (or surface) is a flat or curved side of the shape.
- An **edge** is a line where two faces meet. It may be straight or curved.
- A **vertex** is a point corner where edges meet.

In this section you will learn the properties of a **cube** and a **cuboid** — that is, how many faces, edges and vertices each one has.

[b1] (explanation)
A **cube** is the solid shape you know from a cube of sugar. All of its faces are squares, and they are all the same size.

Look at fig-01, which shows a cube drawn as a see-through solid. Count its parts and you will find these properties:

1. It is a solid shape.
2. It has **6 square faces** — every face is a square.
3. It has **12 edges**.
4. It has **8 vertices**.

A **cuboid** is a solid shape like a match box. Its faces are rectangles, and opposite faces are the same size. Fig-02 shows a cuboid, with leader lines naming its **face**, one of its **vertices** and one of its **edges**. A cuboid has these properties:

1. It has **6 faces**.
2. It has **12 edges**.
3. It has **8 vertices**.

You measure it in cubic units, such as cubic centimetres (cm³) or cubic metres (m³). To find the volume of a cube or a cuboid, you multiply its length, its width and its height together. Think of a cuboid as a stack of cubes. A cuboid that is 4 cm long, 2 cm wide and 3 cm high can be pictured as 3 layers, each layer holding 4 × 2 = 8 cubes. That gives 3 × 8 = 24 cubes, so its volume is 24 cm³. What you have done is simply multiply the three dimensions:
Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height
A cube is just a cuboid whose length, width and height are all the same size. So if a cube has edges of length s, its volume is:
Volume of a cube = s × s × s = s³
A prism is a solid with two identical, parallel faces (its bases) joined by flat rectangular sides. The volume of any prism is found by multiplying the area of one base by the height of the prism:
Volume of a prism = area of base × height
A cuboid is itself a prism whose base is a rectangle, so its base area is length × width, and multiplying by the height gives exactly the same formula as before.    $= lbh$

2. Volume of cube = Length $\times$ Length $\times$ Length

   $= l^{3}$

length $= 3cm$

height $= 8cm$

height $= ?$

$24cm^{3} = 12cm^{2}h$

Divide both side by 12cm$^{2}$

$\frac{24cm^{3}}{12cm^{2}} = \frac{12cm^{2}h}{12cm^{2}}$

$2cm = h$

$h = 2cm$

$V = 3cm \times 3cm \times 3cm$

$V = 27cm^{3}$

"A pyramid is a three-dimensional shape with a flat base that is a polygon and a single top point called the apex. The apex is joined to every corner of the base. A pyramid is named after the shape of its base: the pyramid in fig-03 has a triangular base, so it is a triangular base pyramid (also called a tetrahedron); fig-04 shows a square base pyramid; fig-05 a pentagonal base pyramid; and fig-06 a rectangular base pyramid.

Every pyramid is described by three numbers: its faces (the flat surfaces), its edges (the lines where two faces meet) and its vertices (the corners). The table lists these for the pyramids above:

- Triangular base pyramid: 4 faces, 6 edges, 4 vertices
- Square base pyramid: 5 faces, 8 edges, 5 vertices
- Pentagonal base pyramid: 6 faces, 10 edges, 6 vertices
- Rectangular base pyramid: 5 faces, 8 edges, 5 vertices

The faces always include the base and the side faces. The triangular base pyramid has one triangular base and three triangular sides — 4 faces in all. The square base pyramid has one square base and four triangular sides — 5 faces in all."

Block 2 (explanation):
"A cone is a different three-dimensional shape. Look at the cone in fig-07. It has one flat face, its circular base, and one curved face that narrows up to a point. So the cone has two faces in all: one curved face and one flat face.

The curved face and the flat base meet all the way around in a single curved line, so the cone has one edge. The pointed top where the curved face comes together is a single vertex, so the cone has one vertex.

A cone has 2 faces (1 curved and 1 flat), 1 edge and 1 vertex."

Block 3 (worked_example):
"Worked example — counting the parts of the square base pyramid in fig-04.
Faces: the square base gives 1 face, and each of the four sides of the base carries one triangular face up to the apex. So there are 1 + 4 = 5 faces.
Edges: the square base has 4 edges, and from each corner one edge runs up to the apex, adding 4 more. So there are 4 + 4 = 8 edges.
Vertices: the 4 corners of the base plus the apex give 4 + 1 = 5 vertices.

[b0] (explanation)
The volume of a solid tells you how much space it takes up. You already know the units — when you measure in centimetres, volume is in cubic centimetres (cm³), and when you measure in metres, it is in cubic metres (m³).

For a cuboid, the volume is found by multiplying the area of its base by its height:

Volume of cuboid = area of base × height
                 = length × breadth × height
                 = lbh

Remember that length, breadth and height are all measured in the same unit, and you multiply them together.

A cube is a special cuboid where every edge is the same length, l. So all three dimensions equal l, and

Volume of cube = l × l × l = l³

You can read l³ as "l cubed".

[b1] (explanation)
The same idea — volume equals area of base × height — also works for a prism. A prism has two identical parallel faces joined by a constant cross-section. So for any prism:

Volume of prism = area of base × height

You first find the area of the base face, then multiply it by the height (the distance the prism runs).

[b2] (worked_example)
**Example 1.** Find the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.

Volume of cuboid = L × b × h

length = 3 cm, breadth = 2 cm, height = 8 cm

Volume = 3 cm × 2 cm × 8 cm
       = 48 cm³

So the cuboid has volume 48 cm³.

[b3] (worked_example)
**Example 2.** A cuboid has volume 24 cm³. Its base is 6 cm by 2 cm. Find its height.

Volume of cuboid = L × b × h

length = 6 cm, breadth = 2 cm, height = ?

Volume = 24 cm³

24 cm³ = 6 cm × 2 cm × h
24 cm³ = 12 cm² × h

Divide both sides by 12 cm²:

24 cm³ ÷ 12 cm² = h
2 cm = h

So the height is 2 cm.

[b4] (worked_example)
**Example 3.** Find the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.

Volume of cube = l³

V = (3 cm)³
V = 3 cm × 3 cm × 3 cm
V = 27 cm³

So the cube has volume 27 cm³.

[b5] (worked_example)
**Example 4.** Find the volume of the triangular prism shown in fig-03. Its triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

First find the area of the triangular base:

Area of triangle = ½ × b × h
                = ½ × 5 × 3
                = 7.5 m²

Then volume = area of base × height
            = 7.5 m² × 10 m
            = 75 m³

So the prism has volume 75 m³.

[b0] (explanation)
Two lines are **parallel** when they stay the same distance apart all along their length — they never meet, no matter how far you extend them. In construction we draw parallel lines using a **set square** and a **ruler**.

The trick is that the set square has one straight edge, and the ruler gives you a straight, fixed line to slide the set square along. When you slide the set square along a ruler, the edge of the set square that you draw along keeps the same direction the whole time — so every line you draw with it stays parallel to every other line you draw with it.

Here is the rule to remember: **the ruler does not move, and the set square slides against it.**

You will need: a sharp pencil, a ruler, and a set square from your mathematical set.

[b1] (worked_example)
**Example — construct a line through point P parallel to line AB**

**Step 1.** Draw the line AB with your ruler. Mark a point P anywhere above it. This is the point through which your new parallel line must pass.

**Step 2.** Place the set square so that one of its straight edges lies exactly on the line AB.

**Step 3.** Hold the set square firmly in that position. Place the ruler against one of the *other* edges of the set square, so the ruler is snug against it and the set square can still slide.

**Step 4.** Press the ruler down hard so it does not move. Now slide the set square along the ruler — up toward point P. As you slide, the edge that was on AB stays pointing in the same direction.

**Step 5.** Slide the set square until that edge reaches point P. Draw a line along the edge of the set square through P.

That new line is parallel to AB, because it was drawn with the very same edge of the set square that lay on AB, so both lines have the same direction.

[p0] (practice)

answer: Your new line through Q is parallel to XY because it was drawn with the same edge of the set square that lay on XY, so it keeps the same direction all along — the two lines never meet, no matter how far they are extended.

[p1] (practice)

answer: The ruler must be held still the whole time, and the set square slides along it. The edge of the set square that was on AB keeps its direction as it slides, so the line drawn through P is parallel to AB.

[b0] (explanation)
Two lines are **perpendicular** when they cross at a right angle — a square corner of exactly 90°. You meet perpendicular lines all the time: the floor meets the wall, the page edge meets its top edge, the rungs of a ladder meet the side rails.

You can construct a perpendicular line with just a **ruler** and a **compass** — no measuring of angles needed. The trick is that the compass draws equal distances, and equal distances force the corner to come out exactly right.

Here is the construction to draw a line perpendicular to a given line through a point on it.

**Step 1.** Draw a line and mark a point P on it where you want the perpendicular to stand.

**Step 2.** Put the compass point on P and open it a little. Draw an arc that crosses the line on both sides of P. Where that arc cuts the line, mark the two points A and B. Because you did not move the compass between the two cuts, PA and PB are exactly equal.

**Step 3.** Open the compass a little wider. Put the point on A and draw a small arc above the line. Without changing the compass opening, put the point on B and draw another small arc. The two arcs meet at a point C above the line.

**Step 4.** Join P to C with your ruler. The line PC is perpendicular to the original line.

Why does this work? In Step 3 the point C is exactly the same distance from A as from B. So C is perched perfectly above the middle of the segment AB, and the line from P to C stands straight up from the line — meeting it at exactly 90°.

[b1] (explanation)
Sometimes you need a perpendicular that comes down **onto** the line from a point above it. This is the same idea, flipped around.

**Step 1.** Draw a line and mark a point P **above** the line, off it.

**Step 2.** Put the compass point on P and open it wide enough that the arc will reach the line. Draw an arc that cuts the line in two places. Mark those two cuts A and B.

**Step 3.** Put the compass point on A and draw a small arc below the line. Without changing the compass opening, put the point on B and draw another small arc. The two arcs meet at a point C below the line.

**Step 4.** Join P to C. This line crosses the line at a right angle — it is perpendicular to the line and it passes through P.

Whether the point P sits on the line or above it, the method is the same: mark two equal distances from the line, find the point where the two wider arcs cross, and join. The crossing point is always exactly above the middle of your two marks, which forces the perpendicular.

A good habit before you finish any construction is to look at the corner where the two lines meet. If you have been careful, the corner should look like a clean square corner — and when you check later, it will measure exactly 90°.

[b2] (worked_example)
**Example: construct a perpendicular to line XY at the point P.**

We follow the four steps with the line already drawn and P marked on it.

1. Put the compass point on P and draw an arc that cuts the line at A on the left and B on the right. The compass is not moved between the two cuts, so PA = PB.
2. Widen the compass a little. Draw an arc from A, then an arc from B with the same opening. They cross at C above the line.
3. Use the ruler to join P to C.

The line PC now stands on the line AB at a square corner. We have constructed a perpendicular line at P. If we check the corner with a set square or later construct a 90° angle there, it comes out exactly right because C was found at equal distances from A and B, putting it directly above the middle of AB.

Title: "Finding the Midpoint: Bisecting a Line Segment"

Explanation block:

"When we **bisect** a line segment, we cut it into two equal halves. The point where the two halves meet is called the **midpoint** — it sits exactly halfway along the segment. Bisecting a segment also gives us a line that meets the segment at a right angle (90°), so the line we draw is called the **perpendicular bisector**.

To bisect a line segment you need a ruler and a pair of compasses. Follow these steps:

1. Draw the line segment AB. Open your compass to **more than half** the length of AB.
2. Place the compass point on A and draw an arc that sweeps **above and below** the segment.
3. Without changing the compass opening, place the point on B and draw arcs that sweep above and below, crossing the first two arcs.
4. Use your ruler to join the two points where the arcs cross. This new line is the **perpendicular bisector**. It crosses AB at the midpoint M, and it does so at a right angle, so AM = MB.

Why must the compass be opened more than half the length? If the opening were less than half, the arcs drawn from A and from B would not reach each other, and there would be no crossing points to join. The two crossing points are the key — the line through them is exactly what splits AB into two equal parts."

Worked example:

"**Example: Bisect a line segment 6 cm long.**

1. Draw a line segment AB that is 6 cm long.
2. Open the compass to 4 cm (more than half of 6 cm).
3. With the point on A, draw an arc above and below the segment.
4. Keeping the same opening, put the point on B and draw arcs above and below that cross the first two.
5. Join the two crossing points with a straight line. This is the perpendicular bisector.

The perpendicular bisector crosses AB at point M. Since it cuts AB into two equal parts, AM = MB = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm. Each half is 3 cm long, and the bisector meets AB at 90°."

1. What does the word "bisect" mean when applied to a line segment?
Answer: It means to cut the segment into two equal parts, giving its midpoint.

Answer: 5 cm. Because the bisector cuts PQ into two equal halves, PM = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.

3. When bisecting a segment, the compass must be opened to more than half the segment's length. Explain why.
Answer: So that the arcs drawn from the two ends of the segment reach each other and cross both above and below the line, giving the two crossing points needed to draw the perpendicular bisector. If the opening were less than half, the arcs would not cross.

4. True or false: The perpendicular bisector of a segment meets the segment at a right angle (90°).
Answer: True. "Perpendicular" means at a right angle.

5. A segment is bisected and each half measures 3.5 cm. What was the length of the original segment?
Answer: 7 cm. Because 3.5 × 2 = 7 cm.

6. Practice construction: Draw a segment 8 cm long and bisect it with your compass and ruler. What is the length of each half, and at what angle does the bisector meet the segment?
Answer: Each half is 4 cm long, and the bisector meets the segment at 90°.

[b0] (explanation)
An angle of 60° is special because it is one of the angles you can build using only a ruler and a compass — no protractor needed. It turns out that if you draw an equilateral triangle (a triangle where all three sides are equal), then all three of its angles measure 60°. So the trick is to use the compass to mark a point that is the same distance from two points on your line, and the lines joining them will meet at 60°.

Here is the method, step by step. You will need a sharp pencil, a ruler, and a compass.

Step 1: Draw a straight line and pick a point on it. Let us call the line ℓ and the point A. The angle you build will have its corner (its vertex) at A.

Step 2: Put the point of the compass at A and open it to any convenient width. Draw an arc that crosses the line ℓ. Call the point where the arc meets the line B. Keep the compass at exactly this same width for the next step — do not change it.

Step 3: Keeping the compass at that same width, put its point on B and draw an arc that passes through A and goes up above the line. Where this new arc crosses your first arc, mark that point C.

Step 4: Use the ruler to draw a straight line from A through C and extend it. The angle between your original line ℓ and this new line AC is 60°.

Why does this work? The compass keeps the distance AB the same everywhere, so AB = AC = BC. That makes triangle ABC an equilateral triangle, and every angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°. The angle at A between lines ℓ and AC is therefore 60°.

[b1] (worked_example)
Example: Construct a 60° angle at point P on a line.

1. Draw a line and mark a point P on it. This line will be the bottom side of your angle.
2. Put the compass point on P and open it to a comfortable width (about halfway across your paper is fine). Draw an arc crossing the line to the right of P. Where the arc meets the line, call it Q.
3. Do not change the compass width. Put the point on Q and draw an arc that passes over P and rises up above the line. Where this new arc crosses the first arc, call it R.
4. Use the ruler to draw a straight line from P through R, extending it beyond R.
5. The angle between your original line PQ and the new line PR is 60°.

Check your work: PR is a radius of the first arc, so it equals PQ. And RQ is a radius of the second arc, so it also equals PQ. That means PQ = PR = RQ, so triangle PQR has three equal sides — it is equilateral, and every angle inside it is 60°. The angle you drew at P is the 60° one.

answer: The compass must stay open to the same width as when you drew the first arc (the distance from M to N). Keeping it the same width guarantees that the three sides of the triangle you build are equal, so the triangle is equilateral and every angle inside it measures 60°. The angle you construct at M is therefore 60°.

answer: It is not correct. To get exactly 60° you must keep the compass at the same width for every arc. If you change the width partway through, the three marked points will not all be the same distance from each other, so the triangle will not be equilateral. The angle you draw will no longer be exactly 60° — it could be smaller or larger, but it will not be 60°.

In one morning you might see how many cars pass your house, how many goals your favourite team scored last season, or how much your school spends on books each term. All of these are numbers, but numbers on their own are not very useful. The job of statistics is to turn those scattered numbers into something you can understand and use. Statistics is the branch of mathematics that deals with collecting, organising, analysing, and interpreting data. Data simply means the information or facts that you collect, usually as numbers. The word statistics can mean two things: the whole process of handling data, or the numbers themselves once they have been organised. What is the purpose of statistics? The main purpose is to make sense of information so that we can make better decisions. Statistics helps us in several ways:
  • To summarise large amounts of information. If your teacher lists the marks of all 40 students in your class, that is a lot of numbers. Statistics lets you group them into a table so you can quickly see, for example, how many students scored above 60.
  • To compare. Statistics lets you compare things fairly, such as the attendance of two classes or the rainfall of two months.
  • To spot patterns and trends. When data is organised, you can see whether something is increasing, decreasing, or staying the same over time.
  • To support decisions. Governments, companies, and schools all use statistics to plan. A shop uses sales data to decide which goods to stock; a school uses exam data to decide where learners need more help.
  • To predict. From organised data, you can often make a reasonable guess about what might happen next.
Collecting and tabulating data. The first step in statistics is gathering the data. You can collect it by counting, by measuring, or by asking questions. Once you have the raw data — that is, the data just as you collected it, in no particular order — you organise it into a table. Tabulating means arranging the data into rows and columns so that it is neat and easy to read. A well-made table is the starting point for all the analysis that comes later.

In one morning you might see how many cars pass your house, how many goals your favourite team scored last season, or how much your school spends on books each term. All of these are numbers, but numbers on their own are not very useful. The job of statistics is to turn those scattered numbers into something you can understand and use. Statistics is the branch of mathematics that deals with collecting, organising, analysing, and interpreting data. Data simply means the information or facts that you collect, usually as numbers. The word statistics can mean two things: the whole process of handling data, or the numbers themselves once they have been organised. What is the purpose of statistics? The main purpose is to make sense of information so that we can make better decisions. Statistics helps us in several ways:
  • To summarise large amounts of information. If your teacher lists the marks of all 40 students in your class, that is a lot of numbers. Statistics lets you group them into a table so you can quickly see, for example, how many students scored above 60.
  • To compare. Statistics lets you compare things fairly, such as the attendance of two classes or the rainfall of two months.
  • To spot patterns and trends. When data is organised, you can see whether something is increasing, decreasing, or staying the same over time.
  • To support decisions. Governments, companies, and schools all use statistics to plan. A shop uses sales data to decide which goods to stock; a school uses exam data to decide where learners need more help.
  • To predict. From organised data, you can often make a reasonable guess about what might happen next.
Collecting and tabulating data. The first step in statistics is gathering the data. You can collect it by counting, by measuring, or by asking questions. Once you have the raw data — that is, the data just as you collected it, in no particular order — you organise it into a table. Tabulating means arranging the data into rows and columns so that it is neat and easy to read. A well-made table is the starting point for all the analysis that comes later.

When we collect data we usually just get a long list of numbers, like this: 1, 1, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 1, 2 At a glance it is hard to tell which number comes up most often. So we organise the data. **Tally marks** are a quick way to count how often each value appears. We write one mark for each time a value shows up, and we group the marks in fives — the fifth mark is drawn across the first four, like this: ~~|||~~ (I'll describe: IIII then a diagonal). Actually let me describe: write four vertical marks and the fifth crosses them. After tallying we set the data out in a **frequency table**. The table lists each different value, its tally, and its frequency (the number of times it occurs). From the table we can read the answers to our questions at a glance. Let me do a worked example." [b0] (explanation)
A 90° angle is a right angle — the kind you see at the corner of a book or a sheet of paper. You can construct one exactly with your compasses and ruler, without measuring it. The trick is that a line drawn perpendicular to another line always makes a right angle where it meets it, and the compasses can help you find the point the perpendicular must pass through.

Here is the construction. You will need your compasses, your ruler and a pencil.

**Step 1.** Draw a straight line and label its ends $A$ and $B$. Mark a point $C$ on the line, at the place where you want the right angle to stand.

**Step 2.** Put the point of your compasses at $C$ and draw an arc. This arc cuts the line at two points — label them $D$ and $E$, one on each side of $C$.

**Step 3.** Now open your compasses **wider** than the distance $DC$ from step 2. (The width you used in step 2 will not work here: arcs drawn with it from $D$ and $E$ would only meet again at $C$ itself.) With this new, wider setting, place the compasses at $D$ and draw an arc above the line.

**Step 4.** Keep the compasses at that same wider setting. Move them to $E$ and draw another arc, cutting the first arc at a point $F$ above the line.

**Step 5.** Use your ruler to join $C$ to $F$ with a straight line.

**Step 6.** The line $CF$ is perpendicular to $AB$, so the angle where they meet is a right angle: $\angle FCB = 90^\circ$.

Let us follow the construction through once together, watching what each arc does.

Draw line $AB$. Mark point $C$ in the middle of it. With the compasses at $C$, draw an arc that cuts the line at two points. Call the left one $D$ and the right one $E$ — notice the arc has cut the line exactly twice, once at $D$ and once at $E$.

Now widen the compasses. This is the key move: the new opening must be **larger** than the distance $DC$. With this wider opening, put the point at $D$ and draw a long arc rising above the line. Then, without changing the compasses, put the point at $E$ and draw another arc rising above the line. The two arcs cross each other above the line — that crossing point is $F$.

"To construct an angle of 60° you need only a ruler and a pair of compasses. The trick is to build an equilateral triangle — a triangle whose three sides are all equal. Every angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°, so if you can draw one side of that triangle on your line, the angle at the line is 60°.

Here is how it works. You place a point B on your line and choose one radius for your compass. Because you keep that same radius the whole way through, the three points B, X and A you mark end up exactly the same distance apart. Three equal sides make an equilateral triangle, and that is why the angle you construct is exactly 60°."

Worked example:

Step 2. With centre B and any convenient radius, draw an arc that cuts the line BC at a point. Call that point X.
Step 3. With centre X and the same radius (keep the compass opening unchanged), draw a second arc so that it cuts the first arc. Call the crossing point A.
Step 4. Join A to B with a straight line.
The angle ABC between the line BA and the line BC is 60°."
